stem: During preprocedure review, a client has a Mallampati class I airway assessment. A team member says, “That guarantees intubation will be easy.” Which response by the nurse reflects the best understanding?

options.A: Agree because a low Mallampati class reliably rules out a difficult airway
options.B: Recognize that Mallampati is only one airway predictor; other anatomic and clinical features must also be considered and difficult-airway readiness remains necessary
options.C: Disregard the Mallampati finding completely because it has no relationship to airway difficulty
options.D: Interpret Mallampati class I as evidence that mask ventilation and emergency airway access will also be uncomplicated

rationale: The Mallampati classification is a useful component of preoperative airway assessment, and higher classes are associated with greater intubation difficulty. However, its sensitivity and predictive accuracy are limited when it is used alone. Airway evaluation should integrate other features such as mouth opening, neck mobility, mandibular/thyromental anatomy, prior difficult-airway history, and the broader clinical context. A low Mallampati class therefore does not guarantee easy intubation, mask ventilation, or rescue airway access.
educational_objective: Interpret Mallampati classification as one component—not a stand-alone rule-out test—of difficult-airway assessment and maintain appropriate airway preparedness even when the Mallampati class appears favorable.
source_version_date: Mallampati Score last updated 2025-07-07; current StatPearls 2026 edition
source_locator: Mallampati Score — Continuing Education Activity and Clinical Significance: limited sensitivity/accuracy when used alone; use with complementary airway indicators. Difficult Airway — Anatomy and Physiology: no single test reliably predicts difficulty; assess multiple airway domains and use tools in combination with clinical context.
source_claim_supported: Mallampati is associated with intubation difficulty but is an unreliable stand-alone screening tool and should be interpreted with other airway features and overall clinical context.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential — provide preoperative care; identify risk factors associated with procedures/anesthesia; recognize potential complications and ensure appropriate resources
blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — preoperative airway-risk assessment
correction_summary: Replaced simplistic purpose-of-Mallampati recall with an interpretation item addressing the score's validated limitation as a stand-alone predictor. Avoided numeric cutoffs and corrected the construct toward perioperative risk assessment.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.source_audit: StatPearls Mallampati Score current 2026 edition, last update 2025-07-07, and Difficult Airway chapter verified.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: Association with difficult intubation, limited stand-alone accuracy and need for multiple airway indicators are directly supported.
audit_findings.choice_A: Incorrect; low Mallampati does not reliably rule out difficulty.
audit_findings.choice_B: Correct; accurately states role and limitation of the test.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect; Mallampati still contributes useful risk information.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; one oropharyngeal score does not guarantee success in other airway-management domains.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only B preserves both usefulness and limitation without overclaiming.
audit_findings.cueing: All options interpret the same favorable score rather than comparing unrelated outcomes.
audit_findings.blueprint: Direct preoperative Reduction of Risk Potential fit.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Checked whether class I is always low risk, whether RN scope includes interpreting an airway assessment, and whether mask ventilation is separately predicted; final wording asks understanding/readiness, not independent anesthesia planning.
